solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

parts.note: OR is the heraldic word for gold, so golden gives these letters
a well is a spring of water

explanation.surface: Someone asks who wrote a book called The Golden Spring.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks suggest a book title, but the two words simply give OR (heraldic gold) and WELL (a spring).
explanation.definitionFit: George Orwell was the English author of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four.

clue.text: Breaking of rising clergyman with base in flood

indicators.note: the little word of is broken open so that something can sit between its two letters
in a down clue, rising means the clergyman's title is read upwards, that is backwards

parts.note: REV is short for Reverend, a clergyman
base means low, as in a base or low act

explanation.surface: A vicar on his way up and a lowly base are caught in a flood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' and 'rising' look like part of a flood scene, but 'Breaking' splits the little word 'of' and 'rising' turns the clergyman's title upwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To overflow is to spill over the banks, which is what a flood does.

clue.text: Herb supplied by court physician at opening of Florentine gallery

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them
DR is the abbreviation for doctor, a physician

indicators.note: only the opening part of the gallery's name is kept, the rest being dropped

parts.note: the Uffizi is the famous art gallery in Florence

explanation.surface: A herb is provided by a royal doctor at the opening of an art gallery in Florence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' looks like a royal court but is the verb woo; 'opening of' keeps just UFF from UFFIZI.
explanation.definitionFit: Woodruff is a sweet-scented woodland plant used to flavour drinks, so it counts as a herb.

clue.text: On virgin snow, inversely not best pleased, might one say?

indicators.note: might one say signals that the slang phrase is spoken and heard as a different term

parts.note: not best pleased is pissed off, British slang for annoyed; inversely puts the two words the other way round

explanation.surface: A skier on fresh snow is grumpy about something, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed off' is British slang for annoyed; swapped round by 'inversely' it becomes 'off pissed', which said out loud matches the skiing term.
explanation.definitionFit: Skiing away from groomed runs means going onto untracked, virgin snow.

clue.text: I order M. Clift about, for example

definitions.text: I order M. Clift about, for example

indicators.note: about means moved around, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: Montgomery Clift was a Hollywood film actor

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of bossing the actor Montgomery Clift around on set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' rearranges I ORDER M CLIFT; the whole clue also describes what such a person does with an actor like Clift.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who directs a film tells actors such as Montgomery Clift what to do on set.

parts.note: a group of wolves is a pack
old means aged

explanation.surface: A question about whether elderly wolves are ready to be sent in the post.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as 'old wolves' but the pieces go in the other order: wolves = PACK, old = AGED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something wrapped up and ready to send by mail has been boxed and wrapped for sending.

parts.note: E is East, a point of the compass

indicators.note: to reform is to form again, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A political point about something lasting under a programme of reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' looks like an adjective meaning final, but it is the verb; 'reform' is the signal to rearrange the word 'under'.
explanation.definitionFit: To last is to continue or survive, which is what to endure means.

clue.text: Too much business already — energy zero, dead creature decapitated

parts.note: E is the symbol for energy in physics
nought is zero

indicators.note: its head, the first letter, is cut off

parts.note: the dodo is an extinct bird, a dead creature

explanation.surface: A busy person, out of energy, ponders a beheaded extinct animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decapitated' cuts the first letter from DODO, leaving ODO.
explanation.definitionFit: Having plenty of work on hand already means you are fully occupied and cannot take on more.

parts.note: to black something is to boycott it, as a trade union might
a switch is a thin stick or rod

explanation.surface: A parliamentary official is told to boycott a switch.
explanation.walkthrough: BLACK ROD is the official of the UK House of Lords who summons MPs to the State Opening of Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of a ceremonial officer of the British House of Lords.

clue.text: Get it wrong making us ill at Mecca

indicators.note: making means the following letters are used to make something new by rearranging them

explanation.surface: A pilgrim worries that a trip to Mecca might make us unwell, a bad call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making' is the signal: rearrange US ILL AT MECCA.
explanation.definitionFit: To err in a calculation or judgement is to get it wrong.

clue.text: Relegated sector in Foreign Office's arms?

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: FO is the Foreign Office, and the possessive adds S

indicators.note: a sector is only a part, so a run of letters is taken from inside the word

explanation.surface: A department demoted within the Foreign Office talks about weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sector' signals a part taken from inside 'Relegated', and 'in' places it within the Foreign Office's abbreviation. The definition is cryptic: an animal's front legs could be called its arms.
explanation.definitionFit: The front limbs of a four-legged animal do the work that arms do for a person.

clue.text: Look to become adult, almost, with contemporaries

parts.note: to peer is to look closely

indicators.note: almost means a letter short, so one letter is dropped

parts.note: to grow up is to become an adult

explanation.surface: Someone looks to grow up among people their own age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' drops a letter (the W) from GROW UP to leave GROUP.
explanation.definitionFit: Your peer group is the set of people of your own age and status.

clue.text: Veto removed from feast in which is genealogy of Queen in financial difficulties

indicators.note: the next pieces are placed inside the shortened feast
the first word is taken out of the second

parts.note: a banquet is a feast
a ban is a veto
ER is the Queen (Elizabeth Regina); 'of' adds the possessive S
a family tree is a genealogy

explanation.surface: A banquet without a ban features the Queen's family tree, while someone is short of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Removed from' drops the veto from the feast, and 'in which is' puts the Queen's family tree inside what is left. ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Queer Street is an old British idiom for being in debt or short of money.

parts.note: Oxford is a famous university
a circus is a troupe of entertainers

explanation.surface: Students and circus performers meet at a busy London crossroads.
explanation.walkthrough: OXFORD CIRCUS is a major road junction and Underground station in central London.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the crossing of Oxford Street and Regent Street in London's West End.

clue.text: Dancing when one can fly is not worth bothering about

parts.note: Strictly Come Dancing is a BBC TV dance contest, known simply as Strictly
flying is something meant for ..., so these words give a phrase about ...

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses ballroom dancing as only worth doing if you can fly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strictly Come Dancing' is a popular British TV ballroom show, called 'Strictly' for short.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means trivial or worthless, of no interest to sensible people.

clue.text: Permit about to expire? That's a bit steep

indicators.note: about means going round, so the first piece surrounds the second

parts.note: a grant is a permit or permission
to expire is to die

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a permit about to run out is rather expensive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Permit about to expire' reads as a licence near its end date; really 'about' wraps the permit round the death. 'A bit steep' usually means overpriced.
explanation.definitionFit: A slope or incline is measured by how steep it is.

clue.text: Savage cuts rob p'lice — and others

definitions.text: Savage cuts rob p'lice — and others

indicators.note: savage means wild, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Harsh budget cuts deprive the police and other state services of funding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Savage' rearranges CUTS ROB PLICE; the whole clue is also a comment on austerity hitting state services.
explanation.definitionFit: The state-funded part of the economy, including police, schools and health services.

definitions.meaning: an ancient Greek coin of gold or silver
someone who states something, a declarer

explanation.surface: An old coin is making a pronouncement.
explanation.definitionFit: It names an ancient Greek coin and, whimsically, a person who states or declares.

clue.text: Providing spiritual leader's return to Italian resort

indicators.note: return means both pieces are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: if means providing, as in on condition that
a lama is a Tibetan Buddhist spiritual leader; the 's links it

explanation.surface: A holy man comes back to an Italian holiday spot, providing it suits him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' turns the whole of IF + LAMA backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A town on the Amalfi Coast south of Naples, a popular holiday destination.

clue.text: When insane? The whole of history

definitions.meaning: since long before anyone can remember

explanation.surface: Someone wonders when madness began, and answers: since forever.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means from time immemorial; read literally, it is a period when one is out of one's senses.

indicators.note: in puts the shortened poem inside the vehicle

parts.note: a tram is a car running on rails

indicators.note: most but not all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: an elegy is a mournful poem

explanation.surface: A message, mostly in verse, is read in a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' drops the poem's last letter, and 'in' puts the rest inside a tramcar; 'car' is fair since a tram is also called a tramcar.
explanation.definitionFit: A telegram is a short communication sent by wire.

clue.text: Water expensive, they say, for travellers from Lapland

indicators.note: they say signals that the words are heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: rain is water and dear means expensive

explanation.surface: Lapland visitors grumble that water is costly there.
explanation.walkthrough: RAIN DEAR spoken out loud matches the animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Reindeer are the draught animals of Lapland, pulling sledges, and in legend Santa's sleigh.

indicators.note: catching means holding something inside

parts.note: a net is used to catch things

indicators.note: broken means the letters are smashed and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tries to net a broken toy and will manage it in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' scrambles the toy and 'catching' puts it inside the catcher. The definition works because something not happening now will happen later on.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means not at present but at some later time, in due course.
